procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of acquittal made against the appellant in two cases.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent moved the Magistrate for taking action for contempt of Court because the appellant went back on an undertaking given to the court. The Magistrate directed that the papers be sent to the High Court for appropriate action. The High Court, in revision, after notice to the appellant, held that it was not a fit case for taking action for contempt but set aside the order of acquittal of the appellant and directed that the Magistrate should proceed with the trial from the stage at which respondent No. 1 had been persuaded to not press the complaints.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the judgment of the Bombay High Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision to set aside the acquittal and direct the trial magistrate to proceed with the cases.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal in so far as it related to the offence under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code.

facts: The appellant was acquitted by the trial court for offences under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 13 of the Maharashtra Act.
This acquittal was based on a compounding (a settlement) of the offences between the parties.
The High Court, exercising its revisional powers, set aside the entire acquittal for both offences.
law: An offence under Section 420 IPC can be compounded, but only with the permission of the court.
The offence under Section 13 of the Maharashtra Act was not compoundable.

A High Court can justifiably interfere with an order of acquittal in its revisional jurisdiction in exceptional cases, such as when the acquittal is based on a compounding of an offence that is invalid under the law.
application: The Supreme Court treated the permission granted by the trial magistrate to compound the offences as "one indivisible permission" covering both the Section 420 IPC charge and the Section 13 Maharashtra Act charge.
Since the offence under Section 13 of the Maharashtra Act was non-compoundable, no valid permission could be granted for its compounding.
Because the permission was indivisible, the invalidity of the permission for the Section 13 offence rendered the entire permission invalid.
The Court ruled that it was not permissible to sever the permission into two parts—upholding it for the Section 420 offence while finding it invalid for the Section 13 offence.
The Court reasoned that the magistrate might not have granted permission for the Section 420 offence alone if he had known the case had to proceed anyway on the non-compoundable charge.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument. It held that since the acquittal was based on a single, indivisible, and legally invalid compounding agreement (as one of the offences was non-compoundable), the High Court was justified in setting aside the entire acquittal, including the part related to the offence under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court has the power in its revisional jurisdiction to set aside an order of acquittal.

facts: A trial court acquitted an accused person based on the compounding of an offence.
However, the offence in question was non-compoundable under the law, making the compounding invalid.
The High Court, acting on its own initiative (suo motu), set aside the trial court's order of acquittal.
law: The Supreme Court referenced its prior decision in *K. Chinnaswamy Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh*.
This precedent establishes that a High Court can interfere with an order of acquittal in its revisional jurisdiction in "exceptional cases."

Examples of such exceptional cases include: the trial court lacking jurisdiction, wrongly excluding or admitting evidence, overlooking material evidence, or, crucially, where the acquittal is based on an invalid compounding of an offence.
application: The Court applied the legal principle from the *Chinnaswamy Reddy* case directly to the facts.
It found that the acquittal in this case was based on the compounding of a non-compoundable offence.
This situation is explicitly listed as one of the "exceptional cases" that justifies the High Court's interference.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the acquittal was based on a legally invalid compounding of an offence, the High Court was correct and had the power in its revisional jurisdiction to set aside the order of acquittal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal in so far as it related to the offence under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code.
appellant_arguments: The acquittal for the offense under Section 420 IPC was valid as it was based on a composition agreement between the parties, and the High Court should not have interfered with it.
respondent_arguments: The trial magistrate's order of acquittal was a single order based on a composition of multiple offenses, one of which (under the Maharashtra Ownership of Flats Act) was non-compoundable. Since the composition of a non-compoundable offense is illegal, the entire order based on this composition was not in accordance with the law and was rightly set aside by the High Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court has the power in its revisional jurisdiction to set aside an order of acquittal.
appellant_arguments: The High Court does not have the power in its revisional jurisdiction to set aside an order of acquittal.
respondent_arguments: The High Court has the power in its revisional jurisdiction to set aside an order of acquittal, particularly when the order is found to be not in accordance with the law.

cases.case_name: The State of Kerala v. Narayani Amma Kamala Devi
cases.principle: The High Court's revisional jurisdiction can be exercised by being moved by the convicted person, by any other person, or suo motu on the basis of its own knowledge from any source. All that is necessary to bring the High Court's powers of revision into operation is information that makes the High Court think an order from a Subordinate Court is fit for revision.

cases.case_name: K. Chinnaswamy Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh
cases.principle: The text indicates this case was 'followed', but due to transcription errors in the source text, the specific legal principle for which it was relied upon by the court is not stated.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An acquittal of an accused based on the composition of offenses is not in accordance with the law if one of the offenses is non-compoundable, either with or without the court's permission.
obiter: There is no substance in the contention that the High Court should not have interfered with an acquittal in so far as it related to a specific compoundable offense (like one under s. 420, I.P.C.) when the overall acquittal was based on an unlawful composition.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The trial magistrate's order acquitting the accused, based on a composition of offenses that included a non-compoundable offense, was not in accordance with the law. Because the permission to compound was a single, indivisible permission for both the compoundable and non-compoundable offenses, it was not permissible to sever the permission into two parts. Therefore, the entire order of acquittal was invalid, and the High Court was justified in setting it aside in its revisional jurisdiction.
legal_tests_applied: An order of acquittal can be set aside in revision if it "cannot be said to be 'Jn accordance with law."

When permission to compound offenses is an "indivisible pe~mission for both the offences," it is "not penwssible to sever the permission into two parts and to uphold it for the offence under s. 420, I.P.C., and hold it invalid in respect of the other offence."
The High Court is justified in interfering with a finding of acquittal in revision in cases such as "where the trial court has n6 jurisdiction to try the case but has still acquitted the accused."
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's contention that the High Court should not have interfered with the acquittal for the offense under Section 420 IPC was found to have "no sl!bstance."

The court rejected the idea of partial validity, reasoning that the permission to compound was an "indivisible pe~mission for both the offences" and could not be severed to uphold the acquittal for one offense while invalidating it for the other.
The foundational order of acquittal from the trial magistrate was deemed not "in accordance with law" because it was based on the composition of a non-compoundable offense.
why_respondent_won: The court agreed that the trial magistrate's order acquitting the accused because of the composition of offenses was not "in accordance with law."
The respondent's argument that the composition was illegal was validated, as one of the offenses was "not compoundable with or without the permission of the court."

The High Court's exercise of revisional power to set aside the acquittal was upheld, with the Supreme Court indicating that such interference is justified in cases of fundamental legal error, such as a trial court acting without jurisdiction.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning upholds the principle that an order of acquittal based on a legally impermissible act, such as compounding a non-compoundable offense, cannot be allowed to stand, thereby ensuring the integrity of the judicial process.
The power of the High Court to interfere with an acquittal in its revisional jurisdiction is affirmed as a necessary tool to correct fundamental errors of law and prevent a miscarriage of justice.
